newsitem.title: KENYA: Rwandan refugees die of starvation, U.N. report.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan refugees die of starvation, U.N. report.

text.p: Large numbers of Rwandan refugees are dying of starvation and disease in eastern Zaire after fleeing their camps, the U.N. food agency (FAO) said in a report.
Refugees stranded in east Zaire face the most acute food needs on the continent, said the report issued on Monday and which identified food security problems in 17 African nations.

"The food and humanitarian situation in eastern Zaire is grave. Rwandan refugees are dying of starvation and disease in large numbers, while tens of thousands are severely malnourished and in very poor health," said the report, which advocated donor support for a U.N. airlift.

The U.N. refugee agency has repatriated more than 31,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees from camps south of Zaire's northeastern city of Kisangani, but dozens more die each day -- many from malnutrition-related diseases.

The refugees were among more than 300,000 who fled west in October and November rather than go home when their camps were attacked at the start of a revolt by victorious rebels led by Laurent Kabila who took the capital Kinshasa on Saturday.
Throughout the Great Lakes region there was cause for "serious concern" over food security as ethnic conflict exacerbated existing difficulties, the report said.
In Burundi, despite the relaxation of a regional trade embargo, the food supply situation is tight because of a poor 1997 first season harvest and civil strife.
In Rwanda, the large number of returning refugees and a rapid deterioration of security in areas bordering Zaire has aggravated already precarious food supply.
"Seventeen sub-Saharan African countries are experiencing food shortages and emergencies despite good 1996 harvests in several parts of the continent," the quarterly report added.
Drought and floods are the main causes of food supply problems facing more than three million people in East Africa and the Horn, it said.
The situation is "especially critical" in Kenya's pastoral Eastern Province, while civil strife in northern Uganda and southern Sudan has disrupted food production.

The report entitled Food Supply Situation and Crop Prospects in Sub-Saharan Africa and published in the Kenyan capital is produced as part of the FAO's Global Information and Early Warning System (GIEWS).
"The global food aid availability which in recent years has been on a downward trend is unlikely to improve in the coming years," said FAO's Abdur Rashid.

FAO advocated four measures: aid to the east Zaire refugees, contingency planning in East Africa against emergency should the main rains fail, emergency aid for Burundi, Rwanda, Sierra Leone and Liberia and donor support for an FAO food security programme to enable low-income countries to increase food production.
Despite recent weather setbacks the overall outlook for food supplies in sub-Saharan Africa has improved somewhat, FAO said.
